Who We Serve

Four kinds of practice. Four very different billing problems.

Women's health is not one billing specialty.

A midwife, a birth center, a fertility clinic and a gynecology office get paid by different rules, and a billing company that treats them the same will miss money in all four.

Midwives and birth centers fight for fair payment from Medicaid and managed care plans, deal with facility and professional fee splits, and often work without any billing support. Maternity practices live inside the global obstetric package, where one transfer of care or one missed visit count can change the whole claim.

Fertility clinics bill dozens of lab and procedure codes per cycle, depend on benefit verification that changes by state and employer plan, and carry a large patient-pay balance. Women's health and gynecology practices run on high visit volume, same-day preventive plus problem visits, and procedures that are easy to perform and easy to forget to bill.

PMEX codes from the note in your EHR, submits within 24 hours of the signed visit, and works every denial and underpayment. You keep your EHR. We work inside it.

The Education

Why billing for women's health and maternity care is so hard to get right

Most specialties bill one visit at a time. Maternity care does not. A pregnancy is usually billed as a global package: CPT 59400 for vaginal delivery, 59510 for cesarean, 59610 for vaginal birth after cesarean, and 59618 for cesarean after a trial of labor. Each bundles antepartum care, delivery and postpartum care into one claim that is often filed months after the first visit. If the patient transfers, changes insurance, delivers elsewhere or is co-managed with a specialist, the package has to be split, and a wrong split means a denial or an audit refund request.

Midwifery billing adds a payer problem. Medicare has paid certified nurse midwives at 100 percent of the physician fee schedule since 2011 under the Affordable Care Act, but that parity does not extend to Medicaid. In a survey of state Medicaid officials published in the Milbank Quarterly, states that pay midwives differently from physicians reported paying 70 to 92 percent of the physician rate. Community midwives (certified professional midwives and licensed midwives) face additional enrollment, credentialing and malpractice insurance barriers in many states.

Fertility billing is closer to a lab and procedure business than an office visit business. One IVF cycle can touch egg retrieval (58970), fertilization (89268 or ICSI 89280 and 89281), embryo culture (89250 and 89251), cryopreservation (89258 and 89337), and transfer (58974), plus monitoring ultrasounds and visits. Coverage depends on state mandates, whether the employer plan is fully insured or self-funded, and whether the plan excludes infertility entirely.

Women's health and gynecology brings its own recurring problems: preventive visits billed with a problem visit on the same day, modifier 25 and 59 misuse, IUD and implant device codes billed separately from the procedure, and in-office procedures that never reach the claim.

Medicaid Births About 42%

Share of U.S. births covered by Medicaid, which makes Medicaid rates and enrollment central to maternity and midwifery revenue.

Midwife Rates 70-92%

Range of physician rates paid to midwives in states that pay them differently, per a Milbank Quarterly survey of state Medicaid programs.

CNM Parity 100%

Medicare payment for CNM services relative to the physician fee schedule since the ACA, so Medicare claims should never be paid at the old reduced rate.

Doula Coverage 26 + DC

States reimbursing doula services through Medicaid as of March 2026, each with its own enrollment and billing rules.

The common thread:

In every one of these lines, the money is lost before a denial ever appears. Claims are paid at the wrong level, split wrong, never filed, or paid by Medicaid at a rate that does not cover the care. PMEX audits for all four.

Service Line 1

Midwifery and birth center billing

Independent midwives and birth centers are often one or two clinicians with no billing staff, and the payment system is least friendly to exactly them.

CNM and CM Claims

Professional claims for certified nurse midwives and certified midwives billed under the correct NPI, payer enrollment and supervision or collaboration rules for your state.

CPM and LM Enrollment

NPI, CAQH, Medicaid enrollment and managed care contracting for licensed and certified professional midwives, where state law allows them to bill.

Birth Center Facility Fees

Facility and professional fees reported correctly, so a birth center is not paid only for one while the other is left unbilled.

Transfer of Care Billing

Labor that transfers to a hospital is billed for what was actually provided, because some Medicaid programs pay little or nothing for labor care after transfer if the claim is built wrong.

Home Birth Claims

Coverage verification and claims for home birth where the payer or state Medicaid program covers it, with single case agreements where it does not.

Newborn and Postpartum Care

Immediate newborn care, postpartum visits and lactation support billed where the plan covers them, with coverage checked before the visit.

Doula Benefit Billing

Type 1 and Type 2 NPI billing, state registry and enrollment steps, and managed care contracting for Medicaid doula services.

Global Rate Analysis

We compare what the Medicaid or plan global rate pays against what your visit schedule actually costs, so you can see which payers lose you money.

The reality of midwifery payment:

A study of California community midwives found midwives typically charge $7,000 to $10,000 for perinatal care while Medicaid paid between $0 and $2,800 depending on the managed care plan, and only 22 percent of the midwives interviewed were registered Medicaid providers. A 2020 Milbank Quarterly study found about half of birth centers surveyed said Medicaid payment did not cover baseline costs. PMEX cannot change a state rate, but it can make sure every dollar you are owed is billed, tracked and appealed.

The global package is the single biggest source of preventable maternity denials.

Planning ahead for 2027:

Published summaries of the AMA CPT 2027 update report that the global obstetric codes (59400, 59510, 59610, 59618, 59425 and 59426, among others) are being retired effective January 1, 2027 in favor of reporting antepartum care, labor management, delivery and postpartum care as separate phases. If that holds, maternity claims move from one claim at the end of pregnancy to encounter-level claims throughout, which changes cash flow and contract language. Final codes should always be confirmed in the CPT 2027 code set and in each payer's published policy. PMEX is preparing client contracts, charge masters and billing workflows for the change.

Service Line 3

Fertility, IVF and ART billing

Fertility billing sits between a procedure practice and a laboratory, and the patient usually pays part of it.

Cycle-Level Coding

Retrieval 58970, transfer 58974, culture 89250 and 89251, insemination 89268, ICSI 89280 or 89281, cryopreservation and thaw codes coded from the embryology and procedure record.

ICSI and Insemination Rules

Conventional insemination and ICSI are not billed together on the same oocytes, and the ICSI code depends on how many oocytes were injected.

IUI and Monitoring Cycles

Intrauterine insemination 58322 with sperm preparation, pelvic and transvaginal ultrasound monitoring, and the visits around each cycle.

Benefit Verification

Infertility benefits checked before the first visit: whether the plan is fully insured or self-funded, lifetime or per-cycle limits, diagnosis versus treatment coverage, and medications.

State Mandate Tracking

About twenty states have laws requiring some fertility coverage, and the rules differ widely. California SB 729, for example, took effect January 1, 2026 for fully insured large group plans and does not reach self-funded plans.

Prior Authorization

Authorization for IVF, IUI, genetic testing and medications, tracked against the number of retrievals or cycles a plan allows.

PGT and Lab Split Billing

Embryo biopsy billed by the clinic and genetic analysis billed by the lab, with no duplicate charges and no missed ones.

Packages and Patient Balances

Self-pay packages, shared-risk and refund programs, financing and cycle-level patient statements kept separate from insurance claims so balances are accurate.

Where fertility revenue leaks:

Wrong ICSI code for the oocyte count, bundled lab codes billed as separate lines, medicine and diagnostic visits denied because an infertility diagnosis was linked wrong, and retrieval limits exceeded without anyone tracking them. Annual cryostorage is usually a facility charge, not a CPT service, and belongs on the patient account, not on the insurance claim.

Pain Points

The twelve billing problems we hear most from women's health practices

Global package denials

Split care, transfers and payer changes turn one clean claim into a denial or a refund request months later.

Cash flow gaps

Global billing means a pregnancy is not paid until after delivery, sometimes nine months or more after the first visit.

Medicaid underpayment

Midwife and birth center rates are often a fraction of hospital or physician rates, and global rates may not cover longer visits.

Slow Medicaid and managed care payment

In California, midwives reported waits of up to a year even though Medicaid must pay within 45 days. Disputing late payment is unpaid work.

Enrollment and credentialing delays

Each managed care plan runs its own contracting, and a provider cannot be paid until enrollment is complete.

Birth center licensure and facility billing

Some Medicaid plans require facility licensure or credentialing that small birth centers struggle to afford.

Fertility benefit uncertainty

Coverage depends on state law, employer plan type and plan design, so a patient can start a cycle without knowing what insurance will pay.

Patient balances

Fertility and maternity patients often carry large out-of-pocket amounts that need clear estimates and statements.

Missed procedure charges

In-office procedures, IUD devices and ultrasound components get performed and not billed.

Modifier 25 and 59 denials

Repeated modifier denials get corrected claim by claim without fixing the underlying documentation problem.

Authorization mismatches

Approval does not guarantee payment. Claims deny when the final code, provider, date or units differ from what was authorized.

Lack of billing support

Small midwifery practices handle applications and denials between births, on call, with no billing staff.

Common Questions

Midwifery, maternity, fertility and women's health billing answered

How is a pregnancy billed with a global package?
Routine antepartum care, delivery and postpartum care are billed together under one code, such as 59400 for vaginal delivery or 59510 for cesarean. The claim is usually filed after delivery. If care is transferred or split, different antepartum, delivery and postpartum codes are used instead.
What happens if a patient transfers care mid-pregnancy?
Neither practice provided the whole global service. The sending practice bills antepartum-only care (59425 for 4 to 6 visits, 59426 for 7 or more, or individual E/M visits for 1 to 3), and the receiving practice bills delivery-only and postpartum care. Billing a global by mistake leads to denials or recoupment.
Are the global OB codes changing?
Published summaries of the AMA CPT 2027 update report that the global obstetric codes are being retired effective January 1, 2027 in favor of reporting antepartum care, labor management, delivery and postpartum care as separate phases. Confirm final codes in the CPT 2027 code set and with each payer. PMEX is preparing client workflows for the change.
Do Medicare and Medicaid pay midwives the same as physicians?
Medicare pays certified nurse midwives at 100 percent of the physician fee schedule under the Affordable Care Act. Medicaid does not have the same federal parity requirement, and state rates vary. A survey published in the Milbank Quarterly found states that pay midwives differently reported 70 to 92 percent of the physician rate.
Can you bill for licensed midwives and certified professional midwives?
Yes, where state law and the payer allow it. We handle NPI, CAQH, Medicaid enrollment and managed care contracting, and we bill claims under the rules your state and each plan apply.
How do birth centers bill facility and professional fees?
Freestanding birth centers can have a facility fee and a professional fee for the same birth. We confirm which the payer recognizes, bill each correctly, and track transfers to the hospital, which some Medicaid programs pay little for if billed wrong.
Do you handle doula billing?
Yes. As of March 2026, 26 states and Washington, DC reimburse doula services through Medicaid, with state rules on NPI type, training, registry enrollment and managed care contracting. We handle enrollment and claims for doulas and doula groups.
Which fertility codes do you bill?
Egg retrieval (58970), embryo transfer (58974), culture (89250 and 89251), insemination (89268), ICSI (89280 and 89281), cryopreservation (89258 and 89337), thaw codes, PGT biopsy (89290), intrauterine insemination (58322), plus monitoring ultrasounds and visits.
Can you bill both ICSI and conventional insemination?
Not on the same oocytes. The ICSI code also depends on how many oocytes were injected, with 89280 for 10 or fewer and 89281 for more than 10. We check the embryology record before billing.
How do state IVF mandates affect billing?
About twenty states have laws requiring some fertility coverage, and the rules differ widely. They often apply only to fully insured plans, not self-funded employer plans. California SB 729, effective January 1, 2026, applies to fully insured large group plans. We verify plan type and mandate before treatment.
Do you handle fertility patient balances and packages?
Yes. We keep insurance claims separate from self-pay packages, shared-risk or refund programs, financing and cycle-level patient statements so balances are accurate.
How do you handle well-woman and problem visits on the same day?
We check the note for a separately identifiable problem with its own history and decision-making before modifier 25 is used, and we make sure the preventive code matches the patient's age band.
Which EHRs do you work with?
We work inside your existing EHR, including Athenahealth, Epic, eClinicalWorks, NextGen, Kareo and Tebra, Nextech, Artisan and midwife-focused systems, among others.
What does it cost?
Pricing starts at 2.49% of monthly collections, or from $450 per month. Contact us for a quote based on your provider count and volume of deliveries, cycles or visits.
